name: Dagster Labs, Inc. (formerly Elementl)
origin_detail: Founded 2018 as Elementl by Nick Schrock (founder/CTO; Pete Hunt became CEO in Nov 2022); renamed Dagster Labs in Aug 2023; acquired by Prefect in Jul 2026
openness_notes: Open core: Dagster is Apache-2.0 (16.5k GitHub stars); the commercial product is the hosted Dagster+ service. No relicensing found. After the Prefect acquisition the open-source project is to be 'actively developed, not just maintained'.

exit_events.note: Announced 13 Jul 2026 by founder Nick Schrock; terms undisclosed; ~40 staff joined Prefect; Schrock left; Dagster brand, service and contracts continue

risk_events: Competed for 'nearly a decade' with Airflow/Astronomer and Prefect in a crowded orchestration market
Founder-to-professional CEO transition (Pete Hunt, Nov 2022), rename from Elementl (Aug 2023)
Jul 2026: sold to rival Prefect for undisclosed terms; founder departed; ~40 staff transferred
robustness: The Apache-2.0 code and community survive the company's sale; Prefect has committed to keep developing it under the Dagster brand. As a company, Dagster Labs raised at least a $33M Series B (May 2023) but ended as a small acquisition (about 40 staff) rather than an independent firm.
physical_science_relevance: Asset-based orchestration with lineage is useful for reproducible scientific data pipelines; Dagster is used in some research data platforms.
openness_effect_assessment: A permissive licence won Dagster a loyal data-engineering community (active projects tripled in the year to May 2023) and top-tier VC backing, but did not produce a standalone business at scale; the outcome was consolidation into a fellow open-core rival, with the open-source project preserved.
key_takeaway: Dagster shows the typical end-state for a well-liked but sub-scale open-core tool in a crowded category: no relicensing drama, modest funding, then acquisition by a competitor that keeps the open project alive. Openness protected users' continuity even though investors likely saw a limited return.
